what: Value-conversion cases from FormLogic's committed Python contract, vendored so Softn can
hold its own normalizer to the same answers without depending on formlogic.com.
Softn's softn.py and FormLogic's formlogic.py each carry a _plain(): the function that decides
what a Python value becomes when it leaves the guest. The two were written to be ONE dialect,
because the owner wants Python usable in a Softn app, in a FormLogic automation logic block and
on the Desktop, and that only means anything if a snippet means the same thing in all three. The
failure this guards against is silent: an author moves code between them and non-finite floats,
dict-key coercion or deep structures quietly convert differently, with nothing raising.

vendoredFrom.repo: formlogic.com (sibling checkout; Softn does not depend on it)

taken: The 10 cases of FormLogic's 58 that are about VALUE CONVERSION rather than about how a flow
block is entered: flow-result-normalized, flow-plain-non-finite-in-guest, flow-result-safe-integer,
Each is rewritten from `result = <x>` into `value: <expression>` plus any `setup` it needs,
because Softn has no `result` and no flow entry. The VALUES and the outcomes are unchanged;
`formlogicSource` records the original so the rewrite can be checked by eye.
Three cases marked addedBySoftn cover drift the FormLogic corpus happens not to pin but the
shared _plain decides: the negative safe-integer bound, a dict key of a type neither can coerce,
and a bytes value. They are additions to the shared dialect's test coverage, not to the dialect.

The two nesting cases build their value into an underscore-prefixed module name. A plain name would be app STATE, and the host reads state as the app loads — so the case would be observed on the way into the test rather than at the point the case is about.

A case may set raw:true, meaning its expression already calls softn._plain and the harness must not wrap it again. That is how FormLogic's flow-plain-non-finite-in-guest is kept verbatim: it is about what _plain ANSWERS, not about what crosses, and those differ.
leftOut: The other 48 cases are about the flow/condition/applogic/syntax entry shapes, the bound context
names (inputs, event, app, nodes, upstream, kv), FormLogic's prelude helpers (validators,
compliance, finance, safety), author-line reporting and the instruction budget. None of those
has a Softn equivalent: a Softn app has modules, state and softn.* rather than a context and a
result. Softn's own author-line reporting is pinned by python-contract.test.ts, and its budget
Also left out: Softn's _project(), the LOSSY projection used for mirrored app state. FormLogic
has no counterpart because it has no mirrored state, so it is Softn's alone and not part of the
whenTheyDiverge: This test failing means Softn and FormLogic no longer convert a value the same way. Do NOT
'fix' it by editing whichever side the test points at:
1. Work out which behaviour is right. json.dumps/JSON.stringify is the tie-breaker the two were
built around: non-finite floats become null, dict keys coerce the way json.dumps coerces them.
2. Change BOTH normalizers, or neither, in the same change-set across the two repositories.
3. Re-vendor this file from the FormLogic commit that carries the agreed behaviour and update
The messages are deliberately NOT compared: FormLogic says 'the result holds a set' because its
value is a flow result, and Softn says 'a set cannot cross' because its value is a capability
argument. `names` is the part of the message both have to carry — the type or the limit — and
`raises` is the exception class, which is shared.

cases.pins: A tuple becomes a list; NaN and both infinities become null; an int key and a bool key that collide keep the int spelling and the last value; None becomes "null"; a float key becomes its repr.

cases.formlogicSource: result = [formlogic._plain(float("nan")) is None, formlogic._plain(float("inf")) is None, formlogic._plain(-float("inf")) is None, formlogic._plain(1.5)]
cases.value: [softn._plain(float("nan")) is None, softn._plain(float("inf")) is None, softn._plain(-float("inf")) is None, softn._plain(1.5)]
cases.pins: What _plain ANSWERS inside the guest, which is FormLogic's own case verbatim. Checking only the crossed value would not see this: the boundary turns a non-finite float into null on its own, so a _plain that passed one through would look identical from the host and be different to the app.
The largest integer that crosses as a number.

cases.addedBySoftn: The corpus pins the positive bound only; the shared _plain accepts -(2**53 - 1) too, and a one-sided bound is exactly the kind of thing that drifts.

cases.pins: An integer past the safe range is refused rather than silently losing precision.

cases.addedBySoftn: The corpus's key case has an int key and a bool key that COLLIDE, so the surviving key is the int and the bool branch is never reached. These keys do not collide.
cases.pins: A bool key coerces to "true"/"false", not to "1"/"0".

cases.addedBySoftn: The corpus pins only a large POSITIVE integer, so a bound written as `value <= _SAFE_INTEGER` would pass every test. This is the other side.

cases.pins: A set is refused and the message names the type.
A generator is refused rather than silently consumed or emptied.
A class instance is refused and the message names the author's own class.
A function is refused rather than crossing as null.

cases.addedBySoftn: Neither normalizer has a branch for bytes, so both fall through to the same refusal; pinned because bytes are the value most likely to be given a branch later on one side only.
cases.pins: Bytes are refused, not turned into a repr string.

cases.addedBySoftn: The corpus pins the keys json.dumps CAN coerce; this pins the refusal for one it cannot, which is the other half of the same rule.
cases.pins: A key json.dumps could not coerce is refused, naming the key's type.

v = 1
for i in range(70):

result = v
cases.pins: The depth cap is 64 and it is the normalizer's own, reached before the engine's.

cases.formlogicSource:
v = 1
for i in range(40):
    v = [v]
result = v
cases.pins: Under the cap the normalizer passes it, and the ENGINE then refuses it at its own boundary — which is where FormLogic sees this too. Not the normalizer's behaviour, but the pair's, and the reason the cap alone is not the whole story.
